tldr: A new method that enables "experience backtracking to explore counterfactual futures" on video world models—something impossible in the physical world. It extracts dense, action-level supervision without an extra value model, significantly boosting robot policies.
hero_caption: Addressing the high cost of real-world RL (a) and conventional world-model RL (b) that wastes computation on forward-only rollouts, the proposed Rollback (c) rewinds to past decision points to branch and explore, achieving high search efficiency and dense action credit.
overview:
In robot learning, reinforcement learning using action-conditioned world models (simulators) has attracted major attention. However, prior studies treated world models as direct stand-ins for real environments, rolling out actions forward from start to finish just like physical experiments. This wastes vast computational resources simulating uncritical actions outside the key moments that decide success or failure.

To overcome this, the authors tapped into a unique capability no physical environment affords: rewinding time to past decision points and imagining alternative futures ("counterfactual exploration"). This is the proposed paradigm, "Rollback". It time-travels to critical moments in successful or failed real-robot trajectories, branches into diverse actions via Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), and contrasts their downstream outcomes. By directly comparing actions originating from the exact same situation, it derives precise relative action scores (advantages) without needing a separately learned value model (critic), which is often a source of estimation bias.

Furthermore, the team introduced "test-time physics grounding" by asynchronously linking one real robot with 48 GPUs to continuously fine-tune the world model via LoRA using incoming real-world data, preventing simulator hallucinations. Validated across three challenging real-world tasks—block extraction (Jenga), ball tossing, and tabletop curling—Rollback outperformed the strongest baseline by roughly 11% in success rate and even surpassed average human player performance on ball tossing and tabletop curling within just 8 hours of training.
contributions: Proposed Rollback, a new paradigm that restores latent contexts in world models to branch and explore counterfactual futures from past decision points.

Developed a tree-structured value estimation method that contrasts outcomes among sibling nodes from the same branching point to extract fine-grained, action-level relative evaluation labels (advantages) without training a separate value model.

Built an asynchronous training system uniting real-robot execution, distributed world-model search, policy training, and model adaptation, introducing test-time physics grounding to continually correct model dynamics with real-world data.

Demonstrated 10–12% absolute success rate improvements over the strongest existing baseline on three contact-rich real-world tasks, surpassing average human performance on ball tossing and tabletop curling within 8 hours.

sections.heading: Why Is Forward-Only Replay Just Like the Real World a Bad Idea?
sections.summary: Conventional policy learning with world models simply rolls trajectories forward from scratch, mirroring physical experiments. This fails to concentrate search on critical decision points and makes credit assignment difficult. Rollback overcomes this limitation through backtracking.
sections.details:
Action-conditioned world models are promising simulators that replace the cost of hardware wear and tear and manual human resets. However, existing world-model reinforcement learning had a major blind spot: running forward rollouts from start to finish just like a physical robot, discarding all intermediate temporal contexts.

In the physical world, going back to the moment of failure to try an alternative move is impossible. But in a software-based world model, one can simply reload the cached past internal state (context) and rewind time (Rollback). Leaving this capability untapped is a missed opportunity.

Conventional forward rollouts face three major hurdles:
- **Excessive Wasted Exploration**: Only a fraction of decision points in a task critically influence the outcome. Restarting from scratch wastes compute repeatedly simulating trivial actions.
- **Sparse Action-Level Supervision**: Relying solely on sparse episode-level success makes credit assignment—determining which precise action helped or hurt—extremely difficult. Training a critic to compensate introduces estimation bias and destabilizes learning.
- **World-Model Prediction Bias**: As the policy improves, it encounters out-of-distribution states unseen during pre-training, allowing the policy to exploit physical prediction errors in the simulator.

Rollback resolves all these issues by rolling back to pivotal decision points in real or demonstrated trajectories, conducting Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), and directly contrasting outcomes of alternative actions taken from identical initial conditions.

captions.F1: Comparison of real-world RL (a), forward-only world-model RL (b), and the proposed Rollback (c). Rollback rewinds to critical decision points to branch and directly learns from outcome differences, enabling highly efficient learning.

sections.heading: At the Crossroads of Real-Robot RL, Video World Models, and Tree Search
sections.summary: This section reviews robot policy learning, world models for robotics, model-based RL, and Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). Rollback connects the reversibility of recent diffusion and flow-matching world models to real-robot policy improvement for the first time.
sections.details:
To understand the position of this work, consider its connection across four research domains:

### Interactive Learning for Robot Policies
Applying reinforcement learning (RL) to large foundation models like OpenVLA or π0 using real-world data is an active area (e.g., iRe-VLA, VLA-RL, RECAP). However, trial-and-error on physical hardware suffers from reset overhead and wear, making scaling difficult.

### Emergence of World Models in Robotics
Video generation models acting as simulators (UniSim, IRASim, GE-Sim) are advancing rapidly. Yet, most prior work limited their use to offline policy evaluation or forward synthetic data generation, leaving the reversibility of the simulators untouched.

### Policy Improvement with World Models
Methods like World-Env, WMPO, and RISE perform RL inside world models, but all rely on forward rollouts. In particular, RISE trains an auxiliary progress value model to estimate advantages, risking policy divergence due to value approximation errors.

### Bridging Tree Search and Physical Systems
As seen in AlphaGo, MuZero, and Go-Explore, tree search with backtracking is remarkably powerful in discrete games or perfect physics simulators. Rollback's decisive novelty lies in extending tree search principles to video world models that predict high-dimensional continuous vision and proprioception.

sections.heading: Problem Formulation and the World Model as a Rewindable Environment
sections.summary: We formulate policies that take multi-view images and joint states to output action chunks. By caching and restoring world model internal context, we mathematically define experience backtracking to branch repeatedly without regenerating shared history.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Problem Formulation
Let $g$ be the language goal and $o_t$ be the robot observation at time $t$. Observation $o_t$ contains three multi-view camera images and 16-dimensional robot proprioception (7-DoF per arm plus grippers).
The policy $\pi_\theta$ outputs an action chunk $\mathbf{a}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times d_a}$, representing continuous actions over horizon $H$.

The action-conditioned world model $\mathcal{W}_\phi$ takes the temporal context $m_t$ and proposed action chunk $\mathbf{a}_t$, outputting the next observation and updated context:
$$(\hat{o}_{t+1}, m_{t+1}) \sim \mathcal{W}_\phi(\cdot \mid m_t, \mathbf{a}_t, g)$$
Crucially, $\hat{o}_{t+1}$ **jointly predicts robot joint states and gripper status alongside visual frames**. Without this, the policy would have to infer arm poses purely from ambiguous generated images, causing fine contact tasks to fail. The objective is to maximize the real-world success probability $J(\pi_\theta) = \mathbb{E}[y_\tau]$ with minimal real trials.

### 3.2 World Models as Rewindable Environments
Unlike physical environments, internal context $m_t$ in a world model can be cached explicitly in GPU memory. Reloading context $m_t$ from step $t$ allows instant branching of alternative actions $\mathbf{a}_t'$. The authors define this as "Experience Backtracking".

This provides two key benefits:
- Imagination begins directly at pivotal success or failure moments from physical trials.
- Compute scales only with the new branch length, completely bypassing the cost of regenerating shared trajectory prefixes.

sections.heading: The Rollback Paradigm: Counterfactual Tree Search and Critic-Free Advantage Estimation
sections.summary: We break down Rollback's three core components: (1) MCTS-driven backtracking to critical states, (2) direct advantage binning by contrasting sibling nodes under the same context, and (3) continuous model adaptation via real data (test-time physics grounding).
sections.details:
Rollback establishes a search-and-distill framework—analogous to AlphaGo—running closed-loop between video world models and real robots.

### 4.1 Experience Backtracking Tree Search (MCTS)
Built upon GE-Sim 2.0, Rollback selects seed trajectories from real rollouts or demonstrations, using observations at action chunk boundaries as decision contexts to grow a search tree.

- **Compute Allocation via MCTS**: To navigate continuous action spaces, tree expansion uses progressive widening with PUCT scores, balancing the exploitation of promising branches with the exploration of under-visited alternatives.
- **Policy-Guided Proposals**: Candidate action chunks are sampled from the current policy $\pi_\theta$ conditioned on top-tier quality (highest bin $b=K$).
- **Disagreement-Driven Refinement**: Branches where sibling nodes disagree on outcomes (one succeeds while another fails) yield the highest information gain. Nodes with outcome variance enter a priority queue for additional rollouts until reaching a visit count $n_{\mathrm{conf}}$, mitigating label noise.

### 4.2 Tree-Structured Relative Value Estimation (No Critic Needed!)
The value of each action chunk $\hat{q}(v, \mathbf{a}_i)$ is computed directly as the mean success rate of leaf outcomes within its subtree, evaluated by GE-Sim 2.0's learned World Judge.

Crucially, **values are normalized among sibling nodes originating from the same parent context**:
$$b_i = \left\lceil K \cdot \frac{\hat{q}(v, \mathbf{a}_i)}{\max_{u_j} \hat{q}(v, \mathbf{a}_j)} \right\rceil \in \{1, \ldots, K\}$$
Discretizing relative performance into $K$ bins against the best sibling isolates local action advantage from global task difficulty. Following RECAP, bin label $b$ serves as a conditioning prompt for training a flow-matching policy ($\pi_{0.5}$). At inference, setting $b=K$ alongside Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) generates confident, high-reward actions.

### 4.3 Co-Evolution via Test-Time Physics Grounding
As policies improve, they enter states unfamiliar to the initial world model. If the simulator predicts unphysical behavior (e.g., blocks refusing to fall), policies exploit these errors to harvest invalid high rewards.

To counteract this, trajectories $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{real}}$ gathered by the policy on the robot are continuously used for LoRA supervised fine-tuning (400 steps) and Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD, 100 steps). Termed **test-time physics grounding**, this process continually corrects the simulator's physics specifically along state distributions visited by the policy.

captions.F2: Overall architecture of Rollback: (a) MCTS restoring saved internal states to branch without recomputing shared prefixes, (b) tree-structured value estimation contrasting sibling nodes under identical contexts to discretize advantages directly, and (c) co-evolution loop continuously updating the world model with real-robot execution data.

sections.heading: Continuous Hardware Execution with 48 GPUs: Fully Asynchronous Distributed Infrastructure
sections.summary: A cloud-edge distributed system co-locates GPU-heavy video generation search with real hardware execution without blocking. The robot, search workers, policy learner, and model adaptor interact asynchronously.
sections.details:
Simulating video rollouts inside world models is heavily GPU-bound, whereas physical robot experiments are constrained by wall-clock time and limited hardware units. Synchronous execution—waiting for real data, searching, and pausing for policy training—leaves most resources idle.

Rollback decouples cloud and edge components into a fully asynchronous system.

### 5.1 Three-Tier Architecture: Cloud, Edge, and Device
- **Cloud (48 NVIDIA H200 GPUs)**:
  - **Distributed Search Pool (40 GPUs)**: Each worker maintains a policy replica, a world model, and a local context cache, executing complete search trees internally to eliminate high-bandwidth intermediate tensor transfers.
  - **Co-Evolution Learners (8 GPUs)**: Houses independent trainers for the policy (via DDP) and world model adaptation (LoRA SFT + DMD).
  - **Experience Fabric**: A shared data hub with dual streaming pipelines storing and serving real trajectories alongside tree-derived supervision.
- **Edge Site and Device**: A local runtime near the robot isolates high-frequency control from cloud communication. Trajectories upload to the cloud after each episode while updated policy weights sync in the background.

### 5.2 Local Context Reuse and Version Pinning
Search workers retain all node contexts for an assigned tree in local GPU VRAM, making backtracking to prior decision steps virtually costless.
Furthermore, search trees enforce **version pinning**, holding policy and world-model checkpoints static throughout a tree's lifespan. Updating models mid-tree would distort relative comparisons between sibling nodes. Upon completion, distilled supervision emits directly to the Experience Fabric.

captions.F3: Distributed infrastructure partitioned across cloud, edge, and device. Compute-heavy tree search (40 GPUs) and model training (8 GPUs) operate asynchronously in the cloud, while the physical edge robot continuously collects data without idle delays.

sections.heading: Real-World Experiments: Outperforming Strong Baselines and Surpassing Humans in 8 Hours
sections.summary: Evaluated on an AGIBOT Genie-02 humanoid robot across block extraction, ball tossing, and tabletop curling. Rollback achieved 10–12% absolute success rate gains over the strongest baseline, RISE, and surpassed average human player scores within 8 hours on tossing and curling.
sections.details:
### 6.1 Experimental Setup
Evaluations used the AGIBOT Genie-02 dual-arm humanoid robot across three challenging tasks:
1. **Block Extraction**: Horizontally extracting designated wooden blocks from a tower without collapse (delicate contact and stability).
2. **Ball Tossing**: Throwing a ball into a target bin (velocity modulation and release timing).
3. **Tabletop Curling**: Sliding stones to land closest to a target center in a head-to-head match against a human (strategic placement and impulse control).

Baselines included supervised fine-tuning (SFT), real-world RL (RECAP), and RISE w/ GE-Sim2, the state-of-the-art method running forward rollouts on the identical world model. Compute resources and physical training budgets (~8 hours) were strictly matched.

### 6.2 Main Results: Large Success Rate Margins
Results in Table 1 show consistent advantages across all benchmarks:
- **Block Extraction**: Rollback attained **69.33%** (**+10.67%** over RISE's 58.67%, and +12.00% over RECAP).
- **Ball Tossing**: Rollback attained **40.00%** (**+11.11%** over RISE's 28.89%, and +14.44% over RECAP).
- **Tabletop Curling**: Rollback attained **64.44%** (**+11.85%** over RISE's 52.59%, and +13.33% over RECAP).

Under identical world model foundations, Rollback delivered an average relative boost of 24.0% over RISE's forward rollouts. In ball tossing, where split-second release choices govern outcomes, Rollback yielded a 38.5% relative gain.

### 6.3 Ablation Studies: What Drives the Performance?
Ablations on block extraction (Table 2) underscore the necessity of each component:
- **Static World Model (No Grounding)**: Consecutive successful block extractions dropped sharply from 2.60 to 1.90 as accumulated physics errors broke real-world execution.
- **Direct Reward Learning (Training on single-path leaf outcomes rather than subtree expectations)**: Success rate slipped to 59.33%, demonstrating the noise-reduction value of tree aggregation.

### 6.4 Surpassing Human Player Performance
Comparisons against three human players in direct manual play and teleoperation revealed striking trends. Although teleoperation demonstrations were far below human-level dexterity (16.53% in tossing, 38.94% in curling), Rollback bypassed human manual averages within 8 hours (reaching 40.00% vs. 31.48% human average in tossing; 64.44% vs. 58.39% in curling).

captions.F7: Visualization of experience backtracking search in tabletop curling: (a) rewinding from a pivotal step (step 200) along a real execution (blue dashed line) to simulate alternative throws, contrasting (b) a successful slide reaching the house against (c) a failed attempt falling short under identical contexts.
captions.F8: Impact of test-time physics grounding: (a) A static model without co-evolution (middle) hallucinates stone teleportation, whereas the adapted model (bottom) accurately tracks real stone friction (top). (b) RGB prediction error remains substantially lower across training steps.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Turning World Models into Counterfactual Engines
sections.summary: Rollback shifts world models from passive forward-only simulators to counterfactual engines that question past decisions. Combining tree search with continuous test-time grounding offers a promising foundation for next-generation robot learning.
sections.details:
This work introduced Rollback, a policy improvement paradigm driven by experience backtracking in world models.

By rewinding to critical decision points and aggregating downstream outcomes of alternative actions branched from identical contexts, the framework derives dense, reliable action-level supervision without learning a separate value function. Furthermore, by pairing distributed tree search with real-robot execution through test-time physics grounding, the system continuously corrects physical dynamics along the policy's empirical state distribution, overcoming simulator exploitation.

Across three demanding manipulation, throwing, and competitive tasks on a physical dual-arm robot, Rollback significantly outperformed standard imitation learning and world-model RL, reaching superhuman proficiency within an 8-hour training budget.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation Details, Failure Modes, and Qualitative Analysis
sections.summary: The appendix details the 30Hz control interface, Real-Time Chunking (RTC), MCTS algorithmic implementations, an analysis of four primary failure modes in ball tossing, and qualitative branching behaviors.
sections.details:
### Control Interface and Task Details
The policy processes multi-view camera inputs ($384 \times 512$ across head and wrist views) alongside arm proprioception at 30Hz. At execution time, the policy generates 50-step action chunks using Real-Time Chunking (RTC) with a 6-step communication delay and a replanning stride of 32 steps for smooth trajectory synthesis.

### Failure Mode Analysis
An analysis of physical failures in the ball tossing task (Figure 15) revealed four distinct failure modes:
- **Short** and **Overshoot**: Velocity estimation errors at the release point
- **Rim Bounce**: Minute deviations in the launch angle
- **Failed Release**: Delayed gripper opening
Because each failure mode is governed by a single action chunk in a narrow release window, the ability of Rollback to rewind to that exact window and evaluate alternative actions explains its dramatic improvement.

### Qualitative Search Behavior
As illustrated in Figure 10, four sibling branches stemming from the identical past context produce distinct, clean ballistic arcs, confirming the ability of the policy to explore varied counterfactual futures within the world model.

captions.F10: Comparison of four sibling branches originating from the exact same context in ball tossing. Despite sharing identical past frames, distinct action chunks produce diverse flight paths and bucket interactions.

takeaways: A world model's greatest unique asset is backtracking to past decision points to explore counterfactual futures; contrasting sibling branches from the same context provides precise advantages without a learned critic.
As policies improve, they enter states unseen during pre-training, making test-time physics grounding with real-world data vital to prevent simulator hallucinations.
Decoupling cloud infrastructure (40 GPUs for search, 8 GPUs for training) and edge robots into a fully asynchronous system eliminates idle hardware time.
Even when initialized from sub-optimal teleoperated demonstrations (under half the human success rate), self-play exploration in world models can surpass human performance in just 8 hours.
limitations: Requires training and calibrating a task-specific reward model (World Judge) to evaluate task completion.
World-model prediction errors still accumulate over long-horizon, continuous contact phases.
Evaluations remain confined to single tasks and a single physical robot setup; scaling to multi-task foundation models and multi-robot fleets remains future work.
